## Purpose

<!-- hand:purpose -->
The circulation is the engine's haemodynamic model: four time-varying-elastance heart chambers, four valves, a systemic
Windkessel with systemic veins, a pulmonary arterial and venous bed, a pericardium and the pleural pressure, integrated
every 2 ms. Around that circuit runs a 10 Hz control layer (baroreflex, bolus drug effects, volume events, conditions
such as tamponade), a coronary supply/demand balance and the rules that declare and resolve a cardiac arrest. A
clinician-educator reads it to see why pressures, cardiac output and heart rate move as they do; an embedding developer
reads it for the per-beat truths the monitor and the other organ models consume.
<!-- /hand:purpose -->

## Equations in words

<!-- hand:equations -->
- Each heart chamber's pressure follows a time-varying elastance: the ventricles mix an active term a·Emax·(V − V0)
  with a passive exponential end-diastolic pressure–volume relation, the atria interpolate between Emin and Emax, and
  every chamber adds the pericardial and pleural pressures (Smith 2004 form, tables §2.2; `l2/circ/circuit.ts`).
- The activation a(t) is a double-Hill curve with a peak of 1 (Stergiopulos, Meister & Westerhof 1996); its period is
  a multiple of the Weissler pre-ejection period plus ejection time at the current heart rate, not proportional to RR
  (`l2/circ/activation.ts`, `l2/circ/params.ts`).
- Valves pass forward flow against a linear resistance plus a Gorlin-type quadratic term for any stenosis, and
  regurgitant flow through an orifice law in the effective regurgitant orifice area, smoothed at zero pressure
  difference (Gorlin; ASE 2017; `l2/circ/valves.ts`).
- The systemic arteries are a four-element Windkessel whose compliance falls exponentially with pressure inside a
  clamp of 0.5–3 × its reference value; aortic root pressure is the capacitor pressure plus the characteristic
  impedance times the net flow (`l2/circ/circuit.ts`). Venous, pulmonary arterial and pulmonary venous pressures are
  stressed volume over compliance plus the pleural pressure; the pulmonary venous pressure stands for the PCWP
  (`l2/circ/circuit.ts`).
- The pericardium adds an exponential pressure in the combined ventricular volume plus any effusion, floored at 0
  (tables §2.2; `l2/circ/circuit.ts`); tamponade adds up to 250 mL × severity of fluid (`l2/circ/conditions.ts`).
- Pulsus paradoxus in severe tamponade (E118, target ≥ 10 mmHg, Spodick 2003) is NOT met in rc.4 and no mechanism was
  added. The circuit's own interdependence is right in kind — in severe tamponade venous return is confined to
  ventricular systole and falls back in diastole (the backflow is smallest in inspiration), and each inspiration moves about 6 mL from the left to the right
  ventricle at a fixed total volume — but small: SBP swing 3.4 mmHg (healthy 2.4; the it.fails title still quotes FU-4's 3.1). Measured candidate mechanisms
  (2026-10-23, 250 mL, spontaneous breathing): a larger pleural swing alone (8 / 12 cmH2O → 5.2 / 7.1 mmHg); the
  abdominal pump of the descending diaphragm (pSv rising with the pleural fall, × 1–2); extra-alveolar pulmonary-venous
  pooling; the atria inside the pericardial volume (no gain at matched severity). None reaches 10 mmHg at a
  physiological gain while keeping the healthy swing ≤ 5 mmHg; the one combination that did (a 15 cmH2O effort plus
  an abdominal pump of gain 1: 11.5 mmHg) needs a distressed breathing pattern the MODELED respiratory drive does not
  produce in tamponade (it breathes about 16 × 530 mL). A published model of the same class needs the same two things
  — a large effusion and deep breaths — and attributes the swing to both series and septal (parallel) interaction
  (Ramachandran et al., Theor Biol Med Model 2009;6:15); this circuit has no septum. Owner decision pending.
- Pleural pressure rises with alveolar pressure in a positive-pressure breath and falls with the tidal volume in a
  spontaneous one (`l2/circ/pleural.ts`).
- The baroreflex senses the 1 s low-passed MAP (plus a pulse-pressure term, Chapleau & Abboud 1987) against its set
  point: a fast delayed vagal limb lengthens RR, a slow saturating sympathetic limb scales heart rate, SVR,
  contractility and venous capacity, the set point resets after a sustained offset, and a cardiopulmonary limb answers
  transmural right-atrial pressure (B §4.9, tables §1.1; `l2/circ/baroreflex.ts`). No drug moves the set point, so a
  reflex response to a pressor is emergent (`l2/circ/drugs.ts`).
- Coronary supply scales with coronary perfusion pressure above a zero-flow pressure of 15 mmHg and with the diastolic
  time fraction; demand scales with heart rate, LV systolic pressure, contractility and LV volume above a basal share;
  a deficit lowers contractility and, after a lag, depresses the ST segment (tables §3; Suga 1990;
  `l2/circ/coronary.ts`).
- Bolus drugs act as peak-normalised Bateman curves on the circuit's multipliers, scaled by dose and combined
  multiplicatively (tables §6.2–§6.3; `l2/circ/drugs.ts`).
- An arrest is declared when the myocardium can no longer eject or the continuous MAP stays below 25 mmHg for 60 s;
  return of a pulse needs a CPR coronary perfusion pressure of at least 15 mmHg (Paradis 1990; `l2/circ/arrest.ts`).
- Ventricular ectopy (E133) is a hazard on the beating heart drawn from the same inputs as the arrest hazards plus the
  arterial pH and the ischaemia index: drive D = (sK + sT + spH + sIsch)·(1 + cat) + sCat, each term 0 below its
  threshold (K 6.5 mmol/L, core 40 °C or 32 °C, pH 7.20, the ST-depression deficit) and 1 at the arrest model's own
  threshold for that input (K 8.5, 42 °C, 28 °C, pH 7.00, kIsch 0.1); catecholamine inotropy above 1 multiplies the
  substrate and acts alone only above +1 (exogenous overdose). PVC events arrive at 6·D per minute (≤ 30), as single
  PVCs, couplets or non-sustained runs (3–30 beats) whose share grows with D. MODELED only, never while the arrest
  model holds an arrest; draws come from their own `ectopyHazard` stream (never the ECG's `ectopy` stream, which
  times the escape foci) and none is taken at D = 0, so a healthy patient is unchanged. Runs are non-sustained: VF still comes only from the arrest hazards and the onset draw (Durfey 2017;
  Orchard & Cingolani 1994; Jung 2011; Katritsis 2012; Campbell 2015; weights and the rate [ENG];
  `l2/circ/ectopy.ts`).
- What the heat model takes from the flow (E131): with cardiac output below the flow at which oxygen delivery becomes
  critical (≈ 40 % of resting output), the heat model's skin-perfusion fraction falls (to 0 with no flow) and scales the
  blood-borne core–skin transfer, and the blood model's delivered share of the oxygen demand scales the oxidative
  heat; the vasomotor centre's brain-perfusion gate
  (`brainstemOutF(cbfRel)`, `l2/circ/baroreflex.ts`) also gates sweating and shivering. After an arrest the body
  therefore cools by conduction, about 1 °C/h (`l2/thermal/heat.ts`).
- Blood volume follows Lemmens' indexed rule, 70/√(BMI/22) mL/kg, and the circuit is sized on the weight that rule
  implies (Lemmens 2006, tables §1.3; `l2/body-size.ts`).

### [`l2/body-size.ts`](../../packages/engine-core/src/l2/body-size.ts)

| Name | Value | Unit | Source / tag | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SIZE_REF_KG` | `70` | kg | Surg 2006; tables §1.3 | ONE continuous body-size rule for the adult circulation, shared so the blood model and any later module size the same patient the same way. Pure, deterministic, plain data.  Lemmens' indexed blood volume (Lemmens HJM, Bernstein DP, Brodsky JB. Obes Surg 2006;16:773–6: BV = 70/√(BMI/22) mL/kg of actual weight, the tables' §1.3 rule) makes blood volume proportional to height × √weight. The circulation is sized on the weight at which the band's own per-kg blood volume gives that volume ("size weight"), so blood volume AND resting cardiac output (the isometric §2.2 scaling runs on the size weight) follow one continuous, monotonic curve in weight — no BMI step, with or without a stated height. ANCHOR: the band's default patient (70 kg at the band's default height) is exactly itself, so the default 70 kg adult keeps 4,900 mL (M) / 4,550 mL (F) and every rig that gives no height and 70 kg is bit-identical. 127 kg / 175 cm: size 94.3 kg → BV 6.6 L, CO × 1.35 (tables §1.3). The reference weight of the anchor (the engine's default adult, kg). |

During an arrest the reflex therefore withdraws instead of holding SVR at its ceiling for the whole resuscitation, and the relaxation-phase aortic pressure is set by intrinsic tone plus circulating catecholamines (Paradis 1990's CPP band). | `V_EMPTY_ML` | `5` | mL | West zone 1; [ENG: numerics; V0_LV, the smallest volume a chamber can still eject from] | A compartment cannot give blood it does not hold. A flow OUT of a compartment is scaled by min(1, V / vEmpty) of that compartment's volume (chambers: absolute volume; pulmonary arteries/veins: stressed volume — below it the vessels collapse, West zone 1); the systemic veins and the atria collapse instead of holding a negative transmural pressure (floors in `evaluate`). Without it the passive pressures bottom out (EDPVR → −A, linear atria/pulmonary compliances) while the downstream pressure keeps falling, and a ≈ 3 mL/s forward leak ran the RV, LV and pulmonary bed to NEGATIVE volumes after an exsanguination arrest (VRV −273, VLV −62, VPA −1, VPV −6 mL; CVP −1 to −3.5 on the monitor). `vEmpty` is SIZE-SCALED (profile: 5 mL × W/70, i.e. 0.25 mL in a 3.5 kg neonate): an absolute 5 mL throttled small hearts (neonate CO 0.31 → 0.165 L/min) [ENG: numerics; V0_LV, the smallest volume a chamber can still eject from]. |
